Micro-aeration and leachate recirculation for the acceleration of landfill 
stabilization: Enhanced hydrolytic acidification by facultative bacteria 
Kaili Liu a,1, Longyi Lv a,1,*, Weiguang Li b, Xinyuan Wang a, Muda Han a, Zhijun Ren a, 
Wenfang Gao a, Pengfei Wang a, Xiaoyang Liu a, Li Sun a, Guangming Zhang a,* 
a Tianjin Key Laboratory of Clean Energy and Pollution Control, School of Energy and Environmental Engineering, Hebei University of Technology, Tianjin 300401, PR 
China 
b State Key Laboratory of Urban Water Resource and Environment, Harbin Institute of Technology (SKLUWRE, HIT), Harbin 150090, PR China   
H I G H L I G H T S  
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T  
• Micro-aeration and leachate recircula­
tion accelerate the stabilization of 
landfill. 
• The integrated process promotes the 
enrichment of facultative bacteria. 
• Bacteria that cause hydrolytic acidity 
benefit the stabilizing process. 
• Synergy between methanogens and 
acidifying bacteria is enhanced in inte­
grated process.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Landfill 
Micro-aeration 
Leachate recirculation 
Stability 
Microorganisms 
A B S T R A C T   
The long duration of landfill stabilization is one of the challenges faced by municipalities. In this paper, a 
combination of micro-aeration and leachate recirculation is used to achieve rapid degradation of organic matter 
in landfill waste. The results showed that the content of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) in the hydrolysis phase 
increased significantly and could enter the methanogenic phase quickly. Until the end of the landfill, the removal 
rates of chemical oxygen demand (COD), total phosphorus (TP) and ammonia nitrogen (NH4
+–N) by micro- 
aeration and leachate recirculation reached 80.17 %, 48.30 % and 48.56 %, respectively, and the organic 
matter degradation rate reached 50 %. Micro-aeration and leachate recirculation enhanced the abundance of 
facultative hydrolytic bacteria such as Rummeliibacillus and Bacillus and the oxygen tolerance of Methano­
brevibacter and Methanoculleus. Micro-aeration and leachate recirculation improved the organic matter degra­
dation efficiency of landfill waste by promoting the growth of functional microorganisms.

1. Introduction 
As the final stage of comprehensive waste treatment and disposal, 
landfill remain the dominant technology in developing nations (Yu 
et al., 2022). Although the number of landfills in developed countries (e. 
g., the United States and Japan) had declined since the 1990 s, landfills 
in developing countries continue to increase, and China was expected to 
be the largest landfill country by 2030. As of 2021, China had 644 
landfills that disposed of 77.7 million tons of waste, and landfills 
constitute 45.6 % of environmentally sound treatment plants (NBSC 
(National Bureau of Statistics of China), 2021). Anaerobic landfills do 
not promote microbial growth, resulting in a reduction in the biodeg­
radation rate of organic wastes (Viegas et al., 2021). Many landfills 
stabilize only after decades or centuries of decomposition (Lee et al., 
2022). Landfills occupy a large area, rendering land resources scarcer 
and severely impeding the development of urbanization. In addition to 
occupying a considerable amount of land, landfills also severely limit the 
development of urbanization (Huang et al., 2022). In addition to 
reducing the risk of environmental pollution, the large amount of sta­
bilized land can be used for commercial or residential purposes (Zhang 
et al., 2023). 
Therefore, it is crucial to expedite the stabilization process of land­
fills. As a solution, leachate recirculation could significantly reduce the 
amount of leachate to be treated, increase the water content and 
redistribute nutrients and microorganisms in the landfill layer (Xu & 
Zhang, 2022). The reinjection of leachate into the interior of the landfill 
significantly accelerates waste decomposition and stabilization, in­
creases landfill gas production, and rapidly produces settling. Tong 
et al., (2015) demonstrated the effect of leachate recirculation on the 
hydrolysis of food waste in a leaching bed reactor, finding that it 
increased the possibility that hydrolytic bacteria would come into touch 
with the solid surface. In general, hydrolytic acidification are considered 
rate-limiting steps in the degradation of large particulate organic wastes 
(Vavilin et al., 2010). Several strategies to improve solid-phase solubi­
lity have been reported, where leachate recirculation has been identified 
as one of the key parameters to improve the efficiency of hydrolysis and 
acid production, which helped to improve mass transfer and redistribute 
enzymes and microorganisms (Zhang et al., 2022a, Zhang et al., 2022b; 
Gardner et al., 1993). 
However, excessive leachate recirculation could lead to organic load 
overload and acid accumulation, impeding methane production, espe­
cially for anaerobic bioreactors (Grossule & Lavagnolo, 2020). Stabni­
kova et al., (2008) demonstrated the ability of leachate recirculation to 
extract organic substrates from food waste. However, high concentra­
tions of metabolic intermediates in leachate tended to inhibit and retard 
the hydrolysis process. Wang et al., (2021) reported that the accumu­
lation of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) affects the activity of certain specific 
enzymes and bacteria, thereby inhibiting hydrolysis and acid produc­
tion. Long-term leachate recirculation can also lead to ammonia nitro­
gen accumulation in landfills, inhibiting the degradation of landfill 
waste (Hossain et al., 2009). Previous studies had found that aerobic 
aeration to the interior of landfill piles could reduce this inhibition and 
improve solid waste solubilization and hydrolysis in landfill simulator 
reactors (LSRs) (Ike, 2009; Pinjing, 2011). However, the conversion of 
the entire landfill to an aerobic condition incurs a considerable energy 
cost, rendering it an uneconomical treatment option for practical engi­
neering purposes. 
In recent years, micro-aeration technology has been maturely 
applied in organic wastewater treatment, which can effectively remove 
organic pollutants in wastewater (Yang et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2012). 
(Cottingham et al., 1999) showed that micro-aeration could promote 
nitrification in artificial wetlands, but the removal of total nitrogen (TN) 
was limited by the insufficient carbon source. (Ouellet-Plamondon et al., 
2006) conducted micro-aeration at the inlet end of a horizontal flow 
wetland planted with calabash, and the experimental results showed 
high removal of chemical oxygen demand (COD) and TN. The removal 
rate of H2S reached more than 90 % when domestic wastewater was 
aerated in an upflow anaerobic sludge bed (UASB) (Castro et al., 2023). 
2, 4-dinitrophenol is a raw material for synthetic compounds such as 
pesticides, pharmaceuticals and dyes, and widely exists in industrial 
wastewater. Under the condition of micro-aeration, a large amount of 
oxidoreductase is produced, which leads to the degradation of 2, 4-dini­
trophenol (Zhang et al., 2022a, Zhang et al., 2022b). Micro-aeration can 
improve the activity of microbial hydrolytic enzymes and the removal 
rate of organic matter in the aeration tank in the wastewater treatment 
system, and can enhance the synergistic effect of hydrolyzing bacteria 
and acid-producing bacteria. In addition, micro-aeration results in 
higher diversity and abundance of hydrolyzing bacteria, which im­
proves the hydrolysis of complex organic matter and enhances biode­
gradability (Zhang et al., 2022a, Zhang et al., 2022b). 
In addition, the positive effect of microaeration on the production 
and consumption of VFAs has been progressively demonstrated (Liu 
et al., 2023; Shang et al., 2023). Yu et al., (2020) observed that appro­
priate oxygen increased the rate of hydrolytic acidification during 
blackwater digestion and the abundance of colleague hydrotropic 
methanogenic bacteria was also enriched in this environment. Nguyen 
et al., (2019) discovered that the content of volatile fatty acids was 
reduced in a short period of time by 67.4 %, which promoted the re­
covery of methanogenic performance and enhanced overall system 
stability. According to research, micro-aeration can drive facultative 
anaerobic bacteria to release more extracellular enzymes to improve 
lignocellulosic biomass hydrolysis, hence increasing methane genera­
tion potential (Zheng et al., 2019). Micro-aeration in anaerobic diges­
tion and wastewater treatment processes has received increasing 
attention due to its potential economic and environmental benefits (Cao 
et al., 2022). However, there are few studies on the use of micro-aeration 
in landfills to expedite the decomposition of VFAs accumulated during 
landfilling, and additional research is required. 
Although the positive effect of micro-aeration on acid accumulation 
can be expected, it is currently unclear how the combined air–water 
regulation of micro-aeration and leachate recirculation accelerates the 
stabilization of landfill waste. This paper can provide a scientific refer­
ence for establishing a study on rapid landfill stabilization. 
The recirculation of pretreated leachate allows the neutralizing 
substances of leachate to diffuse throughout the landfill, while micro- 
aeration enables facultative bacteria within the landfill to function, 
and the VFAs accumulated can be rapidly utilized to accelerate the 
stability of the landfill. Therefore, the objectives of this study were: (i) to 
evaluate the effects of leachate recirculation and micro-aeration on the 
landfill stabilization process by monitoring leachate, gas and solids in­
dicators and comparing with conventional anaerobic landfills; (ii) to 
investigate the degradation effects of micro-aeration and recirculation 
systems on accumulated VFAs; and (iii) to investigate the bacterial and 
archaeal community structure of landfill using microbiological high- 
throughput sequencing mechanism of landfill stabilization under com­
bined gas–water conditioning. The results of this study can serve as a 
technical reference for the development of landfill process upgrades and 
contribute to society’s sustainable development. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Feedstock 
The landfill simulation experiments were obtained from domestic 
waste from the dormitory area of the university campus and leftover 
canteen refuse from the cafeteria. The waste was screened and pulver­
ized before landfilling, and the proportions were adjusted according to 
the composition of MSW before being deposited into the landfill simu­
lator. The composition ratios of landfill waste in this simulation exper­
iment are shown in Table 1.

2.2. Design and operation of the experimental device 
The landfill simulation experiment was conducted in 4 landfill 
simulation reactors (LSRs) made of organic glass, as shown in Fig. 1. The 
inner diameter of the LSR is 400 mm and the height is 800 cm. The top of 
the LSR is equipped with an external leachate recirculation pipe and gas 
discharge pipe, which are connected to an external wet gas flow meter to 
facilitate the collection and measurement of the generated landfill 
waste. Two sampling ports are set on the side of the column, upper and 
lower, to facilitate uniform sampling. At a height of 10 cm from the 
bottom of the column, a perforated plate with uniform openings is 
installed, which also serves as a support layer. A leachate collection 
chamber is set up below the perforated plate to facilitate the natural 
outflow of leachate under the action of gravity. Install an aeration pipe 
on the side of the column and connect it to the aeration pump. There is a 
leachate discharge port (10 mm) at the bottom of LSRs, which uses a 
valve to control the outflow of leachate. The generated leachate flows 
into the leachate regulating tank from the collection chamber, un­
dergoes pH adjustment, and then is recirculated to LSRs through a 
peristaltic pump. The effective filling height for the landfill simulation 
experiment is 600 cm, and a layer of 80 mesh nylon mesh and a 5 cm 
gravel layer are laid on the upper layer of the perforated plate to prevent 
leachate from blocking the pipeline. 
The LSR-1 operated without leachate recirculation and aeration, 
representing conventional landfills. The LSR-2 was subjected to micro- 
aeration for 15 min at an aeration rate of 100 L/h. LSR-3 was respon­
sible for effluent recirculation. The frequency of recirculation was three 
days per time, and the volume of recirculated leachate was 2 L. The LSR- 
4 was treated with micro-aeration and recirculation of leachate. The 
aeration rate is 100 L/h, and the aeration time is 15 min; the frequency 
of leachate recirculation is 3 d/times, the recirculation volume was 2 L, 
and the recirculation time was 20 min. According to Table 2, each 
landfill column is operated according to its own process parameters. 
2.3. Analytical methods 
Water content was determined using oven drying at 105 ◦C for 12 h 
to determine weight difference, and organic matter was scorched using a 
muffle furnace KSL-1100X at 600 ◦C, before and after weight difference. 
Conventional indicators such as COD, TP, and NH4
+–N were quantified 
according to the APHA standard method (Leckie et al., 1979). VFA was 
determined according to gas chromatography（GC-2014 (Shimadzu)) 
and pH was analyzed by a pH meter (PHSJ-4F (Leica, China)). UV254 was 
defined as the UV absorbance of the water sample at 254 nm and was 
determined using a Hach DR-5000 UV–visible spectrophotometer 
(Hach, USA) to determine the UV–visible spectrum of the leachate, 
scanning at 200–700 nm. The methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2) 
contents and the biogas produced in the subsequent anaerobic phase 
were measured by a gas chromatography (GC-2014 (Shimadzu)) 
equipped with a thermal conductivity detector. 
2.4. DNA extraction and 16S ribosomal RNA gene quantitative PCR 
(qPCR) 
Samples were collected from the middle and bottom of the landfill 
pile on days 5, 105, and 350 and mixed in equal amounts for subsequent 
DNA extraction. DNA was extracted using the EZNA® Soil DNA Kit 
(Omega Bio-Tek, Norcross, GA, US). DNA concentration and purity were 
checked using a NanoDrop 2000 UV-V is spectrophotometer, and DNA 
extraction quality was checked using 1 % agarose gel electrophoresis. 
For PCR amplification, primer pairs 338F (5′-ACTCCTACGGGAGG­
CAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′) were used 
to amplify the bacterial 16S gene. Primer pairs 524F10extF (TGY­
CAGCCGCCGCGGTAA) and Arch958RmodR (YCCGGCGTTGAVTC­
CAATT) were used to amplify against archaea. Through the use of the 
MiSeq PE300 platform, the final high-throughput sequencing was per­
formed by Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co. (Shanghai, China). 
Analyzing the obtained data was performed using the QIIME II pro­
cedure. A detailed description of the procedure can be found in a pre­
vious study (Lv et al., 2021). Raw sequenced sequences were quality 
controlled using Trimmomatic software and spliced using FLASH soft­
ware. Sequences were ASV clustered based on 97 % similarity using 
UPARSE software. Chimeras were eliminated using UCHIME software. 
Species classification was annotated for each sequence using RDP 
Classifier with 70 % confidence threshold. The alpha diversity of each

2.5. Data analysis 
The structure of the microbial community and environmental vari­
ables in landfill were analyzed using a Monte Carlo test based on 999 
random permutations. The SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sci­
ences) Statistics 22.0 software (IBM, USA) was used for statistical 
analysis. One-way ANOVA and Bonferroni post-tests were used to 
compare the data difference, and the evaluation criterion of significant 
difference was p < 0.05. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Stabilization efficiency of landfill waste 
3.1.1. Solid phase degradation process 
Organisms require a continuous absorption water from the sur­
rounding environment to maintain their growth and metabolic activities 
(Kim et al., 2017). The high moisture content of waste helps microbial 
metabolic processes and increases the rate of waste degradation (Huang 
et al., 2022). The waste with different landfill structures maintained a 
high moisture content (greater than 45 %) (see supplementary mate­
rials). The initial water contents of LSR-1, LSR-2, LSR-3 and LSR-4 at the 
beginning of the experiment were 55.56 %, 55.77 %, 55.67 % and 56.87 
%, respectively. In addition, the moisture content was critical to mi­
crobial activity, and LSR-1 lacking sufficient leachate recirculation and 
oxygen entry, resulted in low water content in the waste, which could 
have a detrimental effect on the biodegradation of organic matter. Based 
on the variation of LSR-3, increasing recirculation volume within a 
specific range had shown to be an effective strategy for reducing evap­
oration and accelerating waste degradation without affecting moisture 
content. Until terminal phase of the landfill experiment, the water 
contents of LSR-1, LSR-2, LSR-3 and LSR-4 were 39.26 %, 41.2 %, 44.01 
% and 45.07 %, respectively. The higher water content was conducive to 
the metabolism of microorganisms, the migration and transformation of 
pollutants in the landfill. 
Organic matter content is related to the biodegradability and sta­
bility of landfill waste (Peng et al., 2022). Insoluble organic matter such 
as fats, proteins and polysaccharides in the solid phase organic matter 
are hydrolyzed to long-chain fatty acids, amino acids and soluble sugars, 
respectively, by extracellular enzymes (Ishigaki et al., 2004). Usually, 
the hydrolysis rate of sugars is faster than that of proteins and fats, and 
thus the hydrolysis of proteins and fats plays a controlling role in landfill 
stabilization, becoming the rate-limiting stage of the whole bioreactor 
landfill stabilization process (Prantl et al., 2006). The organic matter 
content in the initial stages of all four reactors was around 56 % (see 
supplementary materials). After the landfill experiment, the organic 
matter in LSR-1, LSR-2, LSR-3, and LSR-4 fluctuated downward to 45.1 
%, 39.16 %, 38.97 %, and 41.38 %, respectively. Throughout the 
experiment, the waste in LSR-1 showed the least decrease in organic 
matter content, mainly due to the LSR-1 column being an anaerobic 
bioreactor, which created a low pH environment at the initial stages of 
the landfill experiment, inhibiting hydrolysis bacteria, which affected 
the hydrolysis rate of landfill waste. LSR-3, although an anaerobic unit, 
was recirculated by leachate, and the leachate recirculation contained 
suitable pH and certain nutrients, the microorganisms accelerated the 
degradation of macromolecular organic matter under this suitable 
environment. From the analysis of the changing trend of organic matter, 
the degradation effect of landfill waste under anaerobic conditions (LSR- 
1) was the worst. In contrast, LSR-4 with certain leachate recirculation 
and micro-aeration techniques enhanced organic matter degradation 
within the landfill. The results showed that the combined air–water 
conditioning technology of micro-aeration and leachate recirculation 
had a positive effect on accelerating the degradation of organic matter in 
landfill waste. 
3.1.2. Degradation of pollutants in leachate 
The concentration of COD in the leachate generated from the initial 
landfill fluctuated greatly from 8000 to 13000 mg⋅L−1, as shown in Fig. 2 
(a). After 50 days of the landfill, the COD concentration in the leachate 
of each LSR showed a rapid increase, with values reaching 100500 
mg⋅L−1, 921600 mg⋅L−1, 90200 mg⋅L−1, and 876500 mg⋅L−1 for LSR-1, 
LSR-2, LSR-3, and LSR-4 landfill columns, respectively. This was mainly 
due to the decomposition and acidification of the waste in the presence 
of oxygen to produce monosaccharides, amino acids, and glycerol. 
Thereafter, the concentration of COD continued to rise, the reaction 
entered the acidification phase, the production of VFAs increased, and 
the pH decreased. At the 350 d of the experiment, the COD values of the 
four LSRs were 42587 mg⋅L−1, 29412 mg⋅L−1, 35754 mg⋅L−1, and 
27754 mg⋅L−1, respectively. The concentration of COD in LSR-4 was 
significantly lower than that of other LSRs due to the conditioning ef­
fects of micro-aeration and leachate recirculation, which provided a 
suitable environment for microbial growth and promoted the produc­
tion of large amounts of extracellular hydrolytic enzymes by hydrolytic 
acidifying bacteria, thus accelerating the leaching of COD from the 
landfill into the leachate. The trend of COD of LSR-2 and LSR-3 at the 
350 d of the experiment showed that the COD concentration of leachate 
recirculation was greater than that of the micro-aeration group. 
Leachate recirculation helped to increase the leaching and transfer of 
organic matter in landfills, providing a suitable growth environment for 
microbial degradation of organic matter. And after accounting for the 
carbon balance of the solid–liquid-gas phases of the landfill pile, the 
residual carbon contents of the four samples were 59.3 % (LSR-1), 46.2 
% (LSR-2), 347 % (LSR-3), and 24 % (LSR-4), and it was found that the 
solid-phase carbon transfer to the gas-phase carbon of LSR-4 was 60 %, 
which is higher than that in LSR-1, which was the complete control, and 
the transfer of solid-phase carbon was 40 % (see Supplementary Mate­
rial). Micro-aeration and leachate recirculation of LSR-4 has been shown 
to rapidly degrade organic matter during the hydrolysis acidification 
stage, promoting the rapid consumption of products by microorganisms 
in the hydrolysis acidification stage, thereby converting organic matter 
into gaseous form. 
Phosphorus in wastewater exists mainly in the form of primary 
phosphate, and a small amount of organic phosphate exists mainly in the 
form of protein. The elemental phosphorus in landfill waste is relatively 
stable, and only a small amount of phosphorus-containing material is 
decomposed into soluble metaphosphate (HPO4
2−) by relevant micro­
organisms. As shown in Fig. 2(b), the TP concentrations in the four new 
landfill reactors were 262 mg⋅L−1, 241 mg⋅L−1, 240 mg⋅L−1, and 261 
mg⋅L−1, respectively. Due to the relatively low phosphorus demand of 
anaerobic microorganisms, the control group had a constant TP con­
centration. The TP in LSR-1 was reduced by 20.75 %, and a higher 
reduction was not achieved. Until the 350 d of the landfill experiment, 
the total phosphorus concentrations in the four LSRs were 218 mg⋅L−1, 
197 mg⋅L−1, 182 mg⋅L−1, and 152 mg⋅L−1. The micro-aeration process 
conditions had lower TP concentrations than the leachate recirculation 
conditions, and the waste piles were in a partly aerobic and anaerobic 
environment with fast microbial degradation of organic matter. The TP 
removal rate of LSR-4 after intermittent micro-aeration and leachate 
recirculation (48.3 %) was higher than the other experimental groups. 
UV254 is a parameter used to determine the degree of aromatization 
of organic matter present in leachate (Renou et al., 2008). In the initial 
stage, the UV254 of leachate decreased with leachate recirculation and 
leaching of organic matter during landfill waste degradation (Fig. 2(c)). 
The UV254 of leachate in LSR-1, LSR-2, LSR-3 and LSR-4 and the reactor 
reached a maximum on 50 d: 56.6 L⋅(mg⋅m)−1, 53.83 L⋅(mg⋅m)−1, 48.85 
L⋅(mg⋅m)−1 and 45.60 L⋅(mg⋅m)−1. As organic matter degraded in 
leachate, the UV254 values gradually decreased, indicating the stabili­
zation of landfill waste. The UV254 values in LSR-1, LSR-2, LSR-3 and 
LSR-4 were 17.6 L⋅(mg⋅m)−1, 12.13 L⋅(mg⋅m)−1, 9.85 L⋅(mg⋅m)−1 and 
9.85 L⋅(mg⋅m)−1, respectively.

3.1.3. Gas composition 
In terms of gas composition, landfill gas production primarily results 
from the degradation of organic matter in landfill waste. Gas production 
results after 350 d of landfill experiments showed that micro-aeration 
and leachate recharge (LSR-4) had the highest cumulative gas produc­
tion (see supplementary material). Fig. 3 showed the yield and gas 
composition of CO2 and CH4 gases in the landfill gas produced by each 
reactor. The CO2 emissions from each reactor exhibited an increasing 
and then decreasing trend. Around 150 d of the landfill, the CO2 pro­
duction of each group reached the highest peak with the concentration 
of CO2 at 76.6 %, 74.95 %, 68.91 % and 73.73 %, respectively. The 
methane emission of each reactor showed a trend of gradually 
increasing and then slowly decreasing. The maximum methane pro­
duction was also concentrated around 150 d, but its peak concentration 
occurred at the 350 d of the landfill, with 43.91 %, 54.22 %, 52.22 % and 
59.22 % for LSR-1, LSR-2, LSR-3 and LSR-4, respectively. The micro- 
aeration and leachate recirculation group (LSR-4) could enter the 
methanogenic stage faster than the other experimental groups, and the 
methanogenic lag time was shorter. The results indicated that micro- 
aeration can promote the hydrolytic acidification of aerobic microor­
ganisms, resulting in the production of large amounts of CO2. With the 
gradual depletion of O2 in LSR-4, the landfill pile entered a facultative 
anaerobic environment and the facultative microorganisms played the 
main dominant role in decomposing small-molecule acids, which also 
produced large amounts of CO2, but their production was not as large as 
that of the hydrolytic acidification stage. When LSR-4 entered the 
methanogenic stage, the CH4 concentration was higher than the CO2 
concentration, and the CH4 concentration increased gradually and 
gently with the landfill time, indicating that the reactor entered the 
stable methanogenic stage. The methanogenic phase appeared earlier in 
LSR-2 and LSR-3 compared to controls. And the methanogenic stage was

3.2. Hydrolysis acidification of integrated process 
The integrated process group of micro-aeration and leachate recir­
culation had a strong advantage in hydrolysis acidification compared to 
the experimental control group. The organic matter content (41.5 %) in 
the integrated process group on the 150 d was lower than that in the 
control group (51.3 %), indicating that the biodegradation efficiency of 
landfill waste in the integrated process group was higher (see supple­
mentary materials). The catabolism of extracellular hydrolytic enzymes 
within the cell accelerated the conversion of large to small organic 
molecules (Li et al., 2022a, Li et al., 2022b). During the period of 0–150 
d, the organic matter of landfill waste in the integrated process 
decreased by 18 %, while that in traditional landfill decreased by 12 %. 
This also indicated that micro-aeration and leachate recirculation had 
strong advantages in accelerating the efficiency of the hydrolysis stage. 
The accumulation of VFAs during the process of waste stabilization is 
a prominent concern for current research experts. VFAs not only serve as 
products of the hydrolysis acidification stage but also act as substrates 
for the methanogenic stage (Lay et al., 2014). If VFAs accumulate in 
substantial quantities, it can not only lower the pH value but also 
severely disrupt the equilibrium of the hydrolysis-acidification stage, 
impeding the methanogenesis process (Matsuto et al., 2015). Moreover, 
the long-term accumulation of acidic substances seriously affects the 
survival of methanogenic bacteria, which makes the methanogenic stage 
seriously delayed and inhibits the stabilization of landfill (Hettiaratchi 
et al., 2014). Consequently, this study investigated and analyzed the 
relationship between pH and VFAs to examine the mechanism for micro- 
aeration and leachate recirculation to accelerate the stabilization pro­
cess of landfill waste. 
The monitoring of leachate pH constitutes one of the key parameters 
for determining the stage of waste degradation (Vigil et al., 2015). As 
illustrated in Fig. 4(a), the pH values were low (4–6) at the beginning of 
the landfill due to the acidification and hydrolysis process of landfill 
waste. According to Fig. 4(b), the accumulation of VFAs peaked at 
around 150 d. The lower pH of the landfill tended to increase the pro­
portion of free VFAs, while the H+ dissociated from the free-state VFAs 
into the cells could lead to cytoplasmic acidification. Fig. 4(c) revealed 
that acetic acid content reached its maximum value at about 100 d of the 
landfill, owing to the dominant role played by hydrolytic and acidifying 
bacteria in the production of a substantial amount of acetic acid from 
macromolecular organic matter (Chung et al., 2015). In comparison 
with other experimental groups, LSR-4 showed a rapid increase in acetic 
acid content, entering the stage of hydrogen and acetic acid production 
first, thereby demonstrating that micro-aeration and leachate recircu­
lation helped to accelerate acidification within landfill waste. During the 
period of 150–200 d in the landfill, the pH values of LSR-1, LSR-2, LSR-3 
and LSR-4 rapidly reached 7.0, 6.61, 6.81, 6.93 and 7.20, respectively.

3.3. Microbiological mechanism of landfill stabilization 
Samples with different landfill times were selected and the microbial 
communities in the four LSRs were analyzed in different dimensions. 
The correlations between microbial community structure, integrated 
process operating parameters and environmental factors were explored, 
and the mechanism of microbial degradation of landfill waste was 
deeply explored.

3.3.4. Integrated microbial action mechanism for accelerated landfill waste 
stabilization 
In terms of the integrated microbial action mechanism for acceler­
ated landfill waste stabilization, micro-aeration and leachate recircula­
tion created a unique landfill environment with overlapping anaerobic 
and aerobic conditions, which supported the ecological niches of 
anaerobic and facultative bacteria. During the early stages of landfill, 
the microbial community structure inside did not differ much. However, 
the integrated process of micro-aeration and leachate recirculation 
promoted a large enrichment of hydrolytic acidifying bacteria. With the 
increase of landfill time, micro-aeration and leachate recirculation 
gradually increased the abundance and diversity of the microbial com­
munity inside the landfill. 
Small amounts of O2 are introduced into anaerobic landfill envi­
ronments, and cells should first use O2 as an electron acceptor because it 
is thermodynamically more favorable. Microorganisms are able to adapt 
their own metabolic pathways from anaerobic to microaerobic, and the 
metabolic shift is accompanied by changes in energy acquisition. It has 
been shown that under micro-aeration conditions, the acetyl coenzyme 
associated with the synthesis of CO2 undergoes the TCA cycle and is 
further oxidized to CO2 using the electron carrier NADH, which facili­
tates the degradation of organic matter to generate large amounts of 
CO2, allowing the entire reaction process to proceed rapidly (Zhang 
et al., 2021). Some studies have shown that the ATP supplied by Pyruvic 
acid entering the TCA cycle in a micro-oxygen environment is 8 times 
that produced under anaerobic conditions (Li et al., 2022a, Li et al., 
2022b). The micro-aerobic environment formed by micro-aeration will 
enable microorganisms to undergo a complete TCA cycle, providing 
sufficient energy support for microbial proliferation. The dominant 
bacteria in LSR-4, such as Enterococcus, Rummeliibacillus, and Clos­
tridium_sensu_stricto_12, which were anaerobic hydrolytic acidifiers, 
accelerate the microbial degradation of VFAs due to the continuous 
provision of micro-oxygenic environment and energy support, and 
provided substrates for the methanogenic phase. 
Under appropriate micro-aeration conditions, methanogenic bacte­
ria (Methanoculleus and Methanobrevibacter) gradually established oxy­
gen tolerance under alternating micro-aerobic and anaerobic 
environmental conditions, and the dominant role of methanogenic 
bacteria in this environment became more obvious. Additionally, the 
continuous leachate recirculation provided water and nutrients to the 
landfill environment cycle, enabling microorganisms to metabolize and 
proliferate in a suitable environment, which promoted system stability. 
The integrated process of micro-aeration and leachate recirculation can 
also keep the balance between different microbial populations in the 
landfill system also between anaerobic and aerobic, between oxidation 
and reduction reactions, and between substrate and product. 
4. Conclusion 
Micro-aeration and leachate recirculation enhanced the hydrolytic 
acidification of microorganisms and increased the production of TVFAs 
by 53 %. At the end of landfill, the concentrations of COD, TP and 
NH4
+–N in leachate could be reduced from the initial concentration 
change to 78 %, 45 % and 58 %, respectively. The organic matter was 
reduced from 58 % to about 25 %, which was 46 % more efficient than 
the degradation of conventional landfill. The species diversity and 
abundance of hydrolytic acidifying bacteria were increased, which 
could rapidly generate VFAs and produce methane from methanogenic 
substrates, accelerating the landfill stabilization process.
